module_title: Harvesting and Post-Harvest Handling of Medicinal Plants

lessons.title: When and How to Harvest Leaves, Roots, and Bark for Maximum Potency
lessons.body: Harvest at the right time to get the strongest medicine. For leaves, pick in the morning after dew dries but before the sun is hot, around 7-9 AM. This is when essential oils are highest. Harvest leaves just before the plant flowers, because after flowering, energy goes to seeds and leaf potency drops. Use clean scissors or a sharp knife. Never tear leaves with your hands as this bruises them and causes dark spots. For roots, harvest in the dry season when the plant is dormant, usually after the leaves turn yellow or die back. This is when the root stores the most active compounds. Dig carefully with a fork or hoe, starting 20 cm away from the stem to avoid cutting the root. Lift the root, shake off soil, and cut off the stem 2 cm above the root crown. For bark, harvest in spring or early summer when sap flows and bark peels easily. Choose a tree at least 10 years old. Using a sharp knife, cut a vertical strip 5 cm wide and 20 cm long. Only take bark from one side of the tree, never ring the whole trunk, or the tree will die. Peel the bark upward. For all harvests, never take more than one-third of the plant at one time. Leave enough for regrowth. In Africa, many traditional healers harvest during specific moon phases, but scientific studies show that temperature, rainfall, and plant growth stage matter most. Always harvest from healthy plants free of disease or pests. Wear gloves to protect your hands and avoid contaminating the plant. Clean your tools with alcohol before moving to the next plant to prevent spreading disease. After harvest, keep plant parts in a shaded basket, not plastic bags, to avoid sweating and mold.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Sorting Herbs After Harvest
lessons.body: After harvest, clean your herbs quickly to remove dirt, insects, and damaged parts. Do not wash roots, bark, or leaves with water unless they are very muddy. Instead, shake off loose soil and use a soft brush to remove dirt. If you must wash, use clean running water and then dry immediately with a cloth. For roots, scrub with a stiff brush under running water to remove all soil. Then cut roots into small pieces, 2-5 cm long, to dry faster. For leaves, remove any yellow, brown, or diseased leaves. Pick out insects, stones, and other plant material. For bark, scrape off the outer dead layer with a knife, then cut into small strips. Sorting means separating by size and quality. Large, uniform pieces dry evenly. Small pieces dry faster. Remove any foreign matter like twigs, grass, or seeds from other plants. Use a clean table or mat, not the ground, to avoid contamination. Wear gloves and a face mask if you are sensitive to dust. Work in a shaded area to prevent wilting. After cleaning, weigh your herbs to know your yield. For example, 1 kg of fresh leaves may become 200-300 g of dried leaves. Record the weight and date. This helps you track your production. If you are selling, clean herbs fetch a higher price. In many African markets, buyers reject herbs with dirt or mold. So take time to clean properly. Never use chemical disinfectants on herbs you will consume. Natural cleaning with water and brushing is best. After cleaning, move immediately to drying. Do not leave wet herbs in a pile, as they will ferment and rot.

lessons.title: Drying Methods: Sun, Shade, and Solar Dryers
lessons.body: Drying removes water from herbs so they can be stored without mold. The goal is to reduce moisture to 10-12% for leaves and 12-14% for roots and bark. There are three main methods: sun drying, shade drying, and solar dryers. Sun drying is cheapest but not always best. Spread herbs in a thin layer on a clean mat or tray. Place in direct sun for 2-3 days, turning every few hours. But direct sun can destroy essential oils and cause leaves to fade. Use sun drying only for roots and bark, which are tougher. Shade drying is better for leaves and flowers. Hang bundles in a well-ventilated, dark room or under a tree. Air must move freely. It takes 5-10 days. The herbs dry slowly, preserving color and aroma. In humid areas, shade drying may cause mold. Solar dryers are best for Africa. Build a simple box dryer with a clear plastic top and vents. The sun heats the air inside, and hot air rises and escapes, pulling in fresh air. Temperature inside can reach 50-60Â°C, which dries herbs in 1-2 days. You can also use a solar dryer with a black absorbing material. For all methods, test dryness by bending a leaf or root. A dry leaf crumbles; a dry root snaps. If it bends, it needs more drying. Never dry herbs on bare ground or on metal roofs that get too hot. Always label each batch with the date and plant name. Store in a cool, dry place after drying. In West Africa, farmers use raised drying racks to keep herbs off the ground and away from animals. This is a good practice.

lessons.title: Grinding and Powdering Herbs Using a Mortar or Mill
lessons.body: Grinding turns dried herbs into powder, which is easy to use, store, and sell. You can grind with a mortar and pestle, a manual mill, or an electric mill. For small amounts, a mortar and pestle is fine. Use a heavy wooden or stone mortar. Put a handful of dried herbs in the mortar and pound with a twisting motion. Do not pound too hard or you will lose powder. Sift the powder through a fine sieve. Return larger pieces to the mortar and grind again. Repeat until all is powder. For larger amounts, use a manual grain mill or a hammer mill. Adjust the mill to a fine setting. Feed dried herbs slowly. Electric mills are faster but can heat the powder, which may reduce potency. If using an electric mill, grind in short bursts of 10-15 seconds to keep it cool. Always wear a dust mask when grinding, as fine powder can irritate your lungs. Grind in a well-ventilated area. After grinding, let the powder cool before packaging. The finer the powder, the better it dissolves and the more potent it seems. But very fine powder can cake. For most medicinal herbs, a medium-fine powder is best. Store powder in airtight containers, away from light and heat. Use within 6-12 months. In Africa, many traditional healers grind herbs fresh for each patient, but for commercial sales, you need consistent powder. Test your grind by rubbing a small amount between your fingers. It should feel smooth, not gritty. If gritty, grind more. Clean your mortar or mill after each batch to avoid mixing herbs. Use a brush and dry cloth. Never wash with water unless you dry completely. Label each batch with the herb name and grind date.

lessons.title: Packaging and Labeling for Local Sales
lessons.body: Packaging protects your herbs and makes them attractive to buyers. Use clean, dry containers. For small sales, clear plastic bags or zip-lock bags work, but they must be thick and food-grade. For larger sales, use glass jars, plastic tubs, or paper bags with a plastic liner. Never use containers that held chemicals or non-food items. Fill containers to the top to reduce air. Squeeze out excess air from plastic bags before sealing. For powders, use a funnel to avoid spilling. Seal bags with a heat sealer or tape. For jars, close tightly. Label every package. A good label has: the common name and scientific name of the herb, the part used (leaf, root, bark), the net weight in grams or kilograms, the harvest date, the drying method, and your contact information. Also include instructions for use, such as 'Steep 1 teaspoon in hot water for 10 minutes.' If you make health claims, be careful. In many African countries, you cannot claim a herb cures a disease without government approval. Instead, say 'traditionally used for...' or 'supports...'. Add a batch number for traceability. For local sales, you can sell at markets, to herbal shops, or to individual customers. Package sizes: 50g, 100g, 250g, and 500g are popular. Use attractive but simple labels. A printed label looks more professional than handwritten. If you cannot print, write clearly with a permanent marker. Include a 'Best Before' date, usually 12 months from packaging. Store packaged herbs in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. In Africa, humidity is a big problem, so add a small silica gel packet to each container if possible. Never package herbs that are not fully dry, or they will mold. Check each package for holes or tears before selling.

lessons.title: Storing Herbs to Prevent Mold and Loss of Potency
lessons.body: Proper storage keeps herbs potent for 1-2 years. The enemies of stored herbs are moisture, heat, light, and pests. First, ensure herbs are completely dry before storage. If there is any moisture, mold will grow. Store in airtight containers: glass jars with rubber seals, metal tins, or heavy plastic containers. Do not use paper or cardboard alone, as moisture and insects can get in. Keep containers in a cool, dark, dry place. A cupboard away from the stove is good. Ideal temperature is below 25Â°C and humidity below 60%. In humid African regions, use a dehumidifier or place silica gel packets in the storage area. You can also store herbs in a sealed bucket with a lid. Add a layer of charcoal or ash at the bottom to absorb moisture. Never store herbs in the refrigerator unless they are in a completely airtight container, as fridge moisture can cause mold. Check stored herbs every month. Look for signs of mold: white, green, or black fuzz, or a musty smell. If you see mold, throw away the entire batch. Do not try to salvage it. Also check for insects. If you find weevils or beetles, freeze the herbs for 48 hours to kill eggs, then re-dry and store in new containers. For long-term storage, keep herbs whole and grind only what you need. Whole leaves and roots last longer than powder. Label each container with the herb name and date. Use older stock first. Rotate your stock. If you sell, keep a record of what you stored and when. In Africa, many farmers lose up to 30% of their harvest to poor storage. With proper storage, you can reduce losses to less than 5%. Always keep your storage area clean and free of rodents. Use traps or cats if needed. Never store herbs near chemicals, fuel, or strong-smelling items, as herbs absorb odors.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest leaves for maximum potency?
options: A) Early morning after dew dries
B) Midday when sun is hottest
quiz.explanation: Essential oils are highest in the morning after dew dries but before the heat of the day.

quiz.q: When should roots be harvested?
options: B) In dry season when plant is dormant
quiz.explanation: Roots store the most active compounds when the plant is dormant in the dry season.

quiz.q: How much bark can you safely remove from a tree?
options: B) One strip from one side
quiz.explanation: Taking bark from only one side prevents girdling and keeps the tree alive.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after harvesting herbs?
quiz.explanation: Shaded baskets prevent sweating and mold; plastic bags trap moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you not wash leaves with water after harvest?
options: B) It causes mold if not dried well
quiz.explanation: Washing adds moisture that can lead to mold if not dried immediately.

quiz.q: What is the best way to clean roots?
options: B) Scrub with stiff brush under running water
quiz.explanation: Scrubbing under running water removes soil without chemicals.

quiz.q: Why should you sort herbs by size?
quiz.explanation: Uniform pieces dry at the same rate, preventing mold in some pieces.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for dried leaves?
quiz.explanation: Leaves should be dried to 10-12% moisture to prevent mold.

quiz.q: Which drying method is best for leaves?
quiz.explanation: Shade drying preserves color and essential oils better than direct sun.

quiz.q: How can you test if a leaf is fully dry?
quiz.explanation: A fully dry leaf crumbles when bent; if it bends, it still has moisture.

quiz.q: What is a solar dryer?
options: A) A box with clear top and vents
quiz.explanation: Solar dryers use sun heat trapped in a box to dry herbs quickly.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying herbs on bare ground?
options: B) Contamination from soil and animals
quiz.explanation: Bare ground exposes herbs to dirt, insects, and animal waste.

quiz.q: What is the best tool for small-scale grinding?
quiz.explanation: Mortar and pestle is traditional, effective, and does not heat the herbs.

quiz.q: Why should you grind in short bursts with an electric mill?
quiz.explanation: Short bursts prevent heat buildup that can reduce potency.

quiz.q: What should you wear when grinding herbs?
quiz.explanation: A dust mask prevents inhalation of fine powder that irritates lungs.

quiz.q: How fine should medicinal herb powder be?
quiz.explanation: Medium-fine powder is easy to use and does not cake as much as very fine powder.

quiz.q: What is the best container for selling herbs?
quiz.explanation: Glass jars with seals protect from moisture, light, and pests.

quiz.q: What information should be on a herb label?
quiz.explanation: Complete labeling builds trust and provides traceability.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid health claims on labels?
options: A) It is illegal in many countries
quiz.explanation: Many countries require government approval for disease cure claims.

quiz.q: What is a good 'Best Before' date for dried herbs?
quiz.explanation: Dried herbs typically maintain potency for about 12 months when stored properly.

quiz.q: Why add silica gel packets to packaged herbs?
quiz.explanation: Silica gel absorbs moisture, preventing mold in humid conditions.

quiz.q: What are the main enemies of stored herbs?
quiz.explanation: Moisture, heat, light, and pests degrade herbs and cause mold.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for herbs?
quiz.explanation: Cool temperatures below 25Â°C slow degradation of active compounds.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mold in stored herbs?
quiz.explanation: Mold produces toxins that spread throughout the batch, so it must be discarded.

quiz.q: How can you kill insect eggs in stored herbs?
quiz.explanation: Freezing for 48 hours kills eggs and larvae without chemicals.

quiz.q: Why store herbs whole rather than ground?
options: C) They are easier to sell
quiz.explanation: Whole herbs have less surface area and retain potency longer than powder.

quiz.q: What can you add to a storage bucket to absorb moisture?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal or ash absorbs moisture and helps keep herbs dry.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored herbs?
quiz.explanation: Monthly checks allow early detection of mold or pests.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to reduce storage losses in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Raised racks keep herbs off the ground and away from animals and moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you not store herbs near chemicals?
quiz.explanation: Herbs are porous and can absorb strong odors from chemicals.
